stem: A red-zone analysis agent calls get_play_by_play, which returns the full play-by-play of a game as about 40,000 tokens of JSON. The agent only ever needs the plays run inside the 20-yard line. Which fix is most effective?

options.text: Change the tool to accept filters and return only the red-zone plays and the fields they need.
options.explanation: Correct. The cheapest token is one that never enters context. Pruning at the source removes the bloat before it costs anything.

options.text: Move the agent to a model with a larger context window so that several full games fit comfortably.
options.explanation: More room doesn't remove the irrelevant tokens. Cost rises and recall still degrades as context fills.

options.text: Turn on compaction with a low trigger so the play-by-play dumps are summarized on almost every turn.
options.explanation: Summarizing after the fact still pays for the full dump each time, and frequent summaries lose detail.

options.text: Tell the agent in its system prompt to ignore every play that happens outside the opponent's red zone.
options.explanation: The irrelevant plays still fill the context and dilute attention, even if the model tries to ignore them.

stem: A scouting agent's conversation is far below the context limit, but dozens of old search results it has already summarized are still in the history. The rest of the conversation, including the coach's instructions, is still needed. Which technique fits best?

options.text: Compaction, which replaces the older turns of the whole conversation with a summary that Claude writes.
options.explanation: Compaction summarizes everything older, including turns that are still needed. It is meant for conversations nearing the window limit.

options.text: Context editing that clears old tool results and keeps the most recent ones, leaving the rest intact.
options.explanation: Correct. Tool-result clearing removes stale results and leaves placeholders, while the instructions and other turns stay as they are.

options.text: The memory tool, so that Claude writes the old search results into files under the /memories folder.
options.explanation: Memory persists information across sessions. On its own it doesn't remove anything from the current context.

options.text: A fresh session started from scratch, with the coach's instructions pasted again at the top of it.
options.explanation: This discards useful conversation along with the stale results. Targeted clearing keeps what is still needed.

stem: A support agent enables server-side compaction at a token threshold. After each response, the app extracts the text block and appends only that string to its stored history. Compaction appears to happen, but the requests keep growing as if it never did. What is the fix?

options.text: Raise the compaction trigger, because a low threshold makes the API discard its compaction work.
options.explanation: The threshold sets when compaction runs. It doesn't explain why the summary never takes effect.

options.text: Switch to context editing, because compaction only works when the tool runner is driving the loop.
options.explanation: Server-side compaction works on ordinary Messages API requests. The issue is how the response is stored.

options.text: Append the full response content, including the compaction block, rather than only the text string.
options.explanation: Correct. The compaction block replaces the older history on later requests. Keeping only the text throws it away, so the full history is resent.

options.text: Resend custom summarization instructions with each request, so that the API keeps the summary.
options.explanation: Summarization instructions change what the summary says. They don't fix a history that drops the compaction block.

stem: In week 1, a coach told a long-running Agent SDK scouting agent to "flag every 4th-down tendency," in the first user message. By week 9, after several automatic compactions, the agent has stopped flagging them. Which fix is most reliable?

options.text: Turn off compaction and rely on the 1M-token window so that the first message is never summarized.
options.explanation: The session will eventually hit the limit, and a buried early instruction gets less attention as context grows anyway.

options.text: Ask the coach to repeat the instruction in the chat whenever the agent seems to have forgotten it.
options.explanation: This relies on people noticing the drift after it has caused misses. It doesn't make the rule durable.

options.text: Lower the compaction threshold, so that summaries are smaller and each one keeps more of the details.
options.explanation: More frequent compaction means more summarization passes, which gives the instruction more chances to be dropped.

options.text: Put the rule in CLAUDE.md or the system prompt, which are sent on every request after compaction.
options.explanation: Correct. Compaction can drop early instructions, while CLAUDE.md content is re-injected on every request. That is where persistent rules belong.

stem: A team enabled tool-result clearing with a very low trigger, so a few old results are cleared on almost every request. Since then, the prompt-cache hit rate has collapsed and input costs have gone up. What change best addresses this?

options.text: Clear more at once and less often, using clear_at_least and a higher trigger, so the cache breaks less.
options.explanation: Correct. Clearing invalidates the cached prefix from that point. The docs recommend clearing enough tokens at once, using clear_at_least, to make the invalidation worth it.

options.text: Turn off prompt caching entirely, because caching and context editing can't be used in the same request.
options.explanation: They can be combined. The fix is to make each cache break count, not to give up caching.

options.text: Clear tool results on every single turn, so that the prefix always stays small enough to be cached cheaply.
options.explanation: Every clearing invalidates the cache from that point, so clearing more often makes the problem worse.

options.text: Move the older tool results into the system prompt, since cached system prompts are never invalidated.
options.explanation: Rewriting the system prompt changes the cached prefix itself and adds the stale results back into context.

stem: An Agent SDK migration agent repeatedly runs a test suite whose output is thousands of lines, then fixes the failures. After a few cycles, its main context is dominated by old test logs and its fixes start repeating earlier mistakes. The team wants to keep one lead agent driving the migration. Which change best fits?

options.text: Add the test-runner tool to exclude_tools in context editing, so that its output is never cleared.
options.explanation: This does the opposite of what's needed. It guarantees the large test logs stay in context permanently.

options.text: Run each test cycle in a subagent that returns only a short list of failing tests and their errors.
options.explanation: Correct. The verbose output stays in the subagent's own context, so the lead agent's context grows only by a concise report.

options.text: Turn off automatic compaction, so that none of the earlier test results are ever lost by summarizing.
options.explanation: Keeping every log makes the bloat worse, and the session will still run toward the window limit.

options.text: Paste the latest test output into the system prompt each cycle, so it always has the agent's attention.
options.explanation: This changes the system prompt every cycle, which breaks caching, and still fills context with raw logs.

stem: A three-step contract pipeline extracts clauses, scores their risk, then drafts a memo. Today step 2 receives step 1's entire conversation, including the raw contract and every intermediate message, and its risk scores have become erratic. Which change best fits?

options.text: Merge the three steps into one long conversation, so each step can see everything the others did.
options.explanation: This increases the noise each step sees. The problem is too much irrelevant context, not too little.

options.text: Give step 2 a larger and more capable model, so that it can cope with the extra conversation it gets.
options.explanation: A stronger model doesn't remove the irrelevant tokens. Cutting the input addresses the cause directly.

options.text: Pass step 2 only step 1's structured output, the extracted clauses, not step 1's whole conversation.
options.explanation: Correct. In a multi-step workflow each step should get only the inputs it needs, which keeps every context small and focused.

options.text: Enable compaction on step 2, so that step 1's conversation is summarized before scoring begins.
options.explanation: Summarizing the transcript is a workaround. Passing just the structured output avoids the transcript entirely.

stem: A game-planning agent calls get_team_rules once at the start of a session; its result lists constraints the agent must respect all session. The team enabled tool-result clearing, and after clearing first triggered, the agent began breaking those rules. Which change fixes this with the least side effect?

options.text: Set clear_tool_inputs to true, so that the call's parameters are cleared along with its old result.
options.explanation: This clears even more of the call. The rule result would still be removed.

options.text: Lower keep to a single tool use, so the clearing strategy holds on to only the most recent result.
options.explanation: Keeping fewer results makes it more likely the early rules result is cleared, not less.

options.text: Turn off prompt caching, since cached prefixes are what cause old results to disappear from context.
options.explanation: Caching doesn't remove content. The clearing strategy is what replaced the rules result with a placeholder.

options.text: List get_team_rules in exclude_tools so it is never cleared, or move the rules to the system prompt.
options.explanation: Correct. exclude_tools lists tools whose uses and results are never cleared. Constraints that apply all session can also live in the system prompt.

stem: An operations agent is connected to six MCP servers exposing about 150 tools in total, and every schema is loaded on every request. Before the agent does any work, a large share of its context is used, and it sometimes picks the wrong tool. Which approach helps most?

options.text: Merge all 150 tools into one large tool that takes an action name and a free-form JSON payload.
options.explanation: One vague mega-tool makes selection and argument errors more likely and hides each action's schema from the model.

options.text: Move to a model with a larger context window, so all of the tool schemas fit with room to spare.
options.explanation: More room doesn't reduce the noise of 150 schemas, and they still cost tokens on every request.

options.text: Use tool search to load tool definitions on demand, and give each agent only the tools it needs.
options.explanation: Correct. Deferred loading keeps unused schemas out of context, and scoping tools per agent reduces both bloat and wrong selections.

options.text: Delete the descriptions from every tool definition, so that each schema costs fewer tokens to load.
options.explanation: Descriptions are how the model chooses the right tool. Removing them saves tokens but makes selection worse.

stem: A ticket-triage agent for a team's season-ticket office runs all day in a single session. Each lookup returns full customer records, and by afternoon responses are slow and expensive. Which TWO techniques directly reduce context bloat? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Have lookups return a short summary and a record ID, with a separate tool to fetch full details.
options.explanation: Correct. Just-in-time retrieval keeps lightweight references in context and loads details only when needed.

options.text: Enable clearing of old tool results, keeping only the few most recent lookups in the context.
options.explanation: Correct. Stale lookup results are replaced with placeholders, so they stop adding tokens to every request.

options.text: Raise max_tokens so the agent has more room to write its answers about each customer ticket.
options.explanation: max_tokens caps output length. It does nothing about the input context piling up.

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window, so the growing history no longer causes issues.
options.explanation: A larger window postpones the limit but not the cost, latency or quality loss from irrelevant tokens.

options.text: Copy every earlier lookup result into the system prompt, so that those tokens are cached cheaply.
options.explanation: This keeps all the stale data in context and changes the system prompt each time, which breaks caching.

stem: A platform team is writing internal guidance on context-management features for its agent developers. Which TWO descriptions of a technique and its effect are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Context editing clears selected old tool results or thinking blocks and leaves placeholders in their place.
options.explanation: Correct. Clearing removes specific stale content while the rest of the conversation stays word for word.

options.text: Compaction replaces the older turns of a conversation with a summary that Claude writes on the server.
options.explanation: Correct. Compaction summarizes rather than deletes, which keeps a long task inside the window.

options.text: The memory tool summarizes the conversation on the server whenever the context approaches its limit.
options.explanation: The memory tool is client-side file storage that persists notes across sessions. It doesn't summarize anything.

options.text: Subagents share their parent's context window, so everything they read is also visible to the parent.
options.explanation: Subagents run in their own context. Only their final report returns to the parent.

options.text: Server-side context editing rewrites the client's stored history, which the app must then sync locally.
options.explanation: Context editing is applied before the prompt reaches Claude. The client keeps its full, unmodified history and needs no sync.

stem: A film-study agent's answers get vaguer and miss details once its conversation passes about 600,000 tokens, most of it old play-by-play output it no longer needs. A product manager proposes moving to a model with a larger context window. Which response best fits?

options.text: Agree: a larger window gives the model more room, so recall will improve
options.explanation: More room doesn't stop attention spreading thinner over irrelevant tokens. The problem is what's in the window, not its size.

options.text: Remove the irrelevant tokens: prune tool output, clear or compact stale history
options.explanation: Correct. Recall degrades as context fills with noise (context rot). Taking out what the task no longer needs addresses the cause, and it also lowers cost and latency.

options.text: Repeat the key instructions at the end of every user message so they stay visible
options.explanation: This adds tokens without removing the bloat that is causing the degradation.

options.text: Lower the effort level so the model spends less attention on the old content
options.explanation: Effort controls how much the model reasons. It doesn't remove irrelevant content from context.

stem: An agent migrates a club's 400 stats scripts to a new data format over several days and many separate sessions. Each new session re-reads the codebase to work out which scripts are done, sometimes migrating a script twice. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Keep one session open for the whole migration so the history holds all progress
options.explanation: A single multi-day session fills with stale output and invites drift. It also loses everything if the session ends.

options.text: Paste a summary of yesterday's chat into the first message of each new session
options.explanation: Manual summaries are inconsistent and depend on someone remembering. They aren't a durable record of which scripts are done.

options.text: Enable compaction so earlier sessions are summarized automatically into the next one
options.explanation: Compaction summarizes within a conversation. It doesn't carry state into a new session.

options.text: Have the agent keep a progress file, updated per script and read at session start
options.explanation: Correct. Structured notes persisted outside the window survive session resets and give each session an exact, cheap record of what's done.

stem: A draft-prep agent loads the full text of all 300 prospect scouting reports into context at the start of every session "in case they're needed". A typical session touches about a dozen prospects. Which design best fits?

options.text: Keep prospect IDs in context and fetch a full report with a tool when needed
options.explanation: Correct. Just-in-time retrieval keeps only references in context and loads detail when the task needs it, so most sessions stay small.

options.text: Keep loading all reports but enable prompt caching so the repeated text costs less
options.explanation: Caching cuts the price of the repeated text but not its size, so the irrelevant reports still dilute the model's attention.

options.text: Summarize all 300 reports into one long overview and load that at the start of each session
options.explanation: This still front-loads mostly irrelevant content, and the summary loses the detail needed for the prospects that matter.

options.text: Load the reports in alphabetical batches of 50 and clear each batch after a few turns
options.explanation: This shuffles irrelevant content in and out instead of loading only what the session needs.

stem: To save on caching costs, a merchandise chatbot appends every fan's messages to one long shared conversation history. A fan asks about their order and is shown another fan's shipping address. Which change best addresses the root cause?

options.text: Tell Claude in the system prompt never to mention details from other customers
options.explanation: Other fans' data would still be in context, and a prompt instruction doesn't reliably keep it out of answers.

options.text: Clear old tool results more often so fewer addresses remain in the shared history
options.explanation: Clearing reduces exposure but leaves the shared design that mixes users' data together.

options.text: Give each fan their own conversation history, starting a fresh session per user
options.explanation: Correct. Context should be isolated per user. One user's data then never enters another user's request.

options.text: Add an output filter that removes addresses from every response
options.explanation: This also blocks a fan's own address and misses other personal details. The data shouldn't be in the shared context at all.

stem: A fantasy-projection agent calls five stats tools in sequence. Each returns thousands of rows that are only used to compute one final number per player, yet every intermediate result lands in the conversation. Which TWO changes best keep the intermediate data out of context? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Move to a model with a larger context window so the rows fit comfortably
options.explanation: The rows would fit but still crowd out what matters and still cost input tokens on every later turn.

options.text: Use programmatic tool calling so code execution calls the tools and only the final numbers reach context
options.explanation: Correct. When code orchestrates the tool calls, the intermediate results stay inside the execution environment and only the output enters the conversation.

options.text: Enable compaction on every turn so each batch of rows is summarized right away
options.explanation: The rows still enter context first, and constant compaction loses detail and cache reuse.

options.text: Ask Claude to ignore the raw rows and focus only on the final numbers
options.explanation: The rows remain in context whatever Claude is asked to attend to.

options.text: Change the tools to return only the fields the next step needs, truncating and saying so
options.explanation: Correct. Pruning at the source means the noise never enters context, and noting the truncation tells Claude more is available.
